en.title: Brad Bird's Aborted Spirit Movie Paved the Way for Ray Gunn
en.summary: Filmmaker Brad Bird reveals how an unmade animated adaptation of Will Eisner's The Spirit directly influenced his upcoming Netflix project, Ray Gunn. The early struggles with a noir-infused comic adaptation taught valuable lessons for his current sci-fi noir venture.
en.body:
For years, the dream of bringing Will Eisner's iconic comic book character, The Spirit, to animated life occupied a significant space in filmmaker **Brad Bird**'s career. Long before enchanting audiences with **Ratatouille** and **The Incredibles**, Bird, alongside fellow Cal Arts graduate **Jerry Rees**, embarked on an ambitious animated feature adaptation of **The Spirit** in the early 1980s. Working with producer **Gary Kurtz**, they even produced an impressive pencil test animation. However, securing studio backing proved insurmountable. The project's commitment to a tough, noir mystery tone, rather than the more palatable musical numbers or talking animals favored by financiers at the time, made studios hesitant, ultimately leading to the project's abandonment.

This early setback, however, was not a dead end but a crucial stepping stone. The experience of developing a mature, genre-bending animated film that faced commercial resistance deeply informed Bird's subsequent creative endeavors. "We were trying to do something that was really adult and noir and action-oriented," Bird explained, reflecting on the **Spirit** project. "And the world was not ready for that in animation at that time." The lessons learned from this aborted attempt at translating Eisner's world to the screen directly paved the way for his current passion project, **Ray Gunn**.

## From Spirit's Shadow to Ray Gunn's Neon Glow

The DNA of **The Spirit**'s unmade adaptation is palpable in **Ray Gunn**, Bird's upcoming CGI animated film for Netflix. This new project plunges into a world of retro-futurist science fiction and noir mystery, following a private investigator and his alien partner as they solve a case involving a pop superstar. While **The Spirit** aimed for a dark, gritty atmosphere, **Ray Gunn** appears to embrace a similar thematic core of mystery and intrigue, albeit with a distinctively vibrant, futuristic aesthetic. The initial struggles to get a mature animated noir off the ground ultimately provided Bird with the experience and conviction to finally realize his vision years later, albeit with a different title and a fresh coat of digital paint.

## A Long Road to Noir Animation

For fans of **Brad Bird**'s unique storytelling and his ability to blend genres with masterful execution, the connection between **The Spirit** and **Ray Gunn** offers a compelling narrative arc of perseverance. The fact that Bird’s ambition for adult-oriented animated features was met with resistance decades ago highlights the evolving landscape of animation and audience expectations. This journey underscores the director's consistent drive to push boundaries within the medium. The eventual greenlighting of **Ray Gunn**, a project that clearly carries echoes of his earlier aspirations, is a testament to his unwavering commitment to bringing complex, genre-infused stories to the screen. It’s a win for fans who have long admired Bird’s knack for sophisticated animation.

## What's Next

**Ray Gunn** is slated for release on Netflix, though a specific release date has not yet been announced. Fans can anticipate further details and potential trailers in the coming months as the film gears up for its debut.

content_raw: After a string of blockbusters in animation, including Ratatouille and both Incredibles movies, as well as Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol in live action, filmmaker Brad Bird is finally getting the chance to make his dream project via Ray Gunn . The upcoming Netflix release is a blend of retro futurist science fiction and noir mystery, with the CGI animated project following the titular gumshoe (voiced by Sam Rockwell) and his alien partner Eyera (Tom Waits) as they investigate a case involving pop superstar Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson).  Ahead of Ray Gunn ’s release, we got the chance to speak to Bird about an older unmade film he worked on previously, an adaptation of Will Eisner’s legendary comic book series The Spirit . Written and drawn by Eisner throughout the 1940s and ‘50s, the original comic followed a private investigator without superpowers named Denny Colt who had been pronounced dead. Using his “resurrection” to build a supernatural mythology around himself, the Spirit went after criminals who slipped through the law’s cracks. In the early 1980s, Bird and fellow Cal Arts grad Jerry Rees began work on an animated feature of The Spirit with Star Wars producer Gary Kurtz. An impressive pencil test animation was completed, but a studio backer could not be found. The fact that the cartoon project was geared more toward tough action/noir mystery than funny animals/songs made financiers nervous, so it was abandoned.  Bird went on to make a name for himself on television with Family Dog and The Simpsons . Eventually he took another stab at getting a more mature animated feature off the ground in the early ‘90s with Ray Gunn , which began as a hand-drawn, two-dimensional project at Turner Pictures, then at Warner Bros. before the latter studio had him pivot to The Iron Giant . With Ray Gunn now resurrected with action-packed footage presented to the public, it becomes clear that lead character Raymond Gunn definitely has Denny Colt vibes. In essence, this is a transmutation of Brad Bird’s original concept for The Spirit .  “I wasn’t consciously aware of it, but it was an unscratched itch,” admits Bird of that project’s retro pulp detective vibe. The concept for Ray Gunn was sparked by the director misinterpreting the B-52’s song “Planet Claire” (“she drove a Plymouth Satellite, faster than the speed of light”), which he mistook for the theme song from 1950s TV show Peter Gunn . The crossed wires led his mind to picture a detective like Gunn in a science fiction context. As Bird elaborates, “Based on misunderstanding a song, I just started piling ideas into it. It wasn’t until later that I figured out, ‘Oh, it’s because you didn’t get to make The Spirit .’ It’s different from The Spirit in a lot of ways, but there was something about noir.
